PHSCS 587

Channel-length modulation

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a simple channel-length-modulation correction adds a slope after saturation

In a real device, a stronger drain field changes the drain-side high-field region and the effective conducting channel. A current labeled saturated can therefore have a finite output slope. This effect is distinct from carrier velocity saturation.

A simple local fit is ID ≈ ID,sat[1 + λCLM(VDS − VDS,sat)] for VDS ≥ VDS,sat. The coefficient λCLM has units V⁻¹. Subtracting the saturation voltage makes the correction equal one at the regional boundary, so the joined current is continuous.

This piecewise model has a slope change at the join. It is a teaching approximation, not a smooth compact model or a first-principles extraction of effective channel length. DIBL, mobility change and series resistance may also affect a measured output characteristic.

Example

With ID,sat = 20 μA, VDS,sat = 0.5 V and λCLM = 0.10 V⁻¹, increasing VDS to 1.1 V gives ID ≈ 21.2 μA. The local output conductance is about 2 μS.

Practice

1. Why must λCLM have inverse-voltage units?

The factor multiplying ID,sat must be dimensionless.

λCLM multiplies a voltage difference inside 1 + λCLMΔV, so its units are V⁻¹.

2. Does a positive post-saturation slope demonstrate carrier velocity saturation?

Separate a changing effective channel from the speed of a carrier.

No. Channel-length modulation concerns the drain-side channel and field geometry. Velocity saturation concerns the carrier velocity versus field; either may influence a real device.
